solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Speed measurement for some circuits showing vehicle's a failure

blocks.note: a gig is a light two-wheeled horse-drawn carriage; the 's is just 'is'
taken as written
a flop is a failure

explanation.surface: Some electronic circuitry is shown up as a failure by a car's performance figures.
explanation.definitionFit: A gigaflop is a billion floating-point operations per second, a unit for rating the processing speed of computer chips.

clue.text: Who's going to support reserve performance?

indicators.note: something going is on the move, so the letters of the word before it are moved about
in a down clue a piece that supports another sits beneath it, so this comes second

blocks.note: ice means coolness or reserve of manner
the letters of WHOS rearranged

explanation.surface: A question about who will back up a substitute's performance.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is read in grid order: the rearranged letters of 'Who's' sit underneath the word for reserve.
explanation.definitionFit: An ice show is a theatrical entertainment staged on a skating rink, so it is a kind of performance.

clue.text: Something put in Christmas pudding is poisonous

definitions.note: read with 'Something': a poisonous thing, a noun

indicators.note: what is put in something sits inside it, so look within the next words

blocks.note: the end of the first word runs into the start of the second

explanation.surface: A warning that an ingredient in the Christmas pudding is toxic.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is 'Something ... poisonous', split around the hidden-word device.
explanation.definitionFit: An asp is a venomous snake, the kind that killed Cleopatra, so it is a poisonous creature.

clue.text: Dean's flower lady?

blocks.note: surface reading: a woman who does the flowers for the dean of a cathedral
setter's reading: a dean (or dene) is a small wooded valley, so this is a bloom belonging to a valley whose name is also a girl's name

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dean' looks like a cathedral official, but it is the old word for a narrow valley; the flower's name is also a woman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The plant is a spring woodland flower with small white bells, and its first word is a common girl's name, hence 'lady'.

clue.text: Some wine put down

blocks.note: first meaning: cheap, ordinary wine in British slang
second meaning: to set something down heavily

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a wine being criticised; plonk is British slang for cheap wine.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a slang noun for inexpensive wine and also a verb for dropping something down with a thud.

clue.text: Army corps on the wagon right away? That's correct

indicators.note: something sent away is no longer present, so the right-hand letter goes

blocks.note: the Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers, a corps of the British Army
someone on the wagon is off drink, or dry
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A question whether an army unit should give up drink immediately, answered with a yes.
explanation.walkthrough: REME is the British Army's corps of engineers who repair kit; 'right away' looks like 'at once' but means drop the R.
explanation.definitionFit: To remedy a fault is to put it right, so the verb is a synonym of correct.

clue.text: No value in report scrapped, which could be this

indicators.note: something scrapped is broken up, so the phrase's letters are taken apart and rebuilt

blocks.note: all fifteen letters are used

explanation.surface: A report is scrapped for being worthless.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition points at the clue itself: the word 'which' is an example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Grammatically, 'which' introduces a relative clause, making it an example of this part of speech.

clue.text: Inmates trod carelessly in cooler

indicators.note: something done carelessly is messy, so the letters are scattered into a new order

blocks.note: all eleven letters are used

explanation.surface: Prisoners walk heedlessly in a prison cell, the cooler being slang for jail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooler' looks like slang for prison, which fits the inmates, but it is the definition in its sense of less friendly.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who is cooler towards you is more aloof, so the phrase is an idiomatic synonym.

clue.text: Tenor in party getting Chinese duck

blocks.note: a do is a party
the Ming dynasty of China
a duck is a score of nought in cricket, so the letter O

explanation.surface: A singer at a party is served Chinese duck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chinese duck' reads as one dish but splits into two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Plácido Domingo is a famous Spanish operatic tenor, so the answer is an example of a tenor.

clue.text: Order new Apple for friendly writer

indicators.note: to order things is to arrange them, so the letters are put into a fresh sequence

blocks.note: N is the abbreviation for new
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone buys a new Apple computer to keep up a correspondence.
explanation.definitionFit: A pen pal is someone you exchange friendly letters with, so they are a writer of a sociable kind.

clue.text: Solid complex houses odd liquid containers

indicators.note: something complex is intricate and tangled, so the letters are mixed up
a thing that houses another holds it inside

blocks.note: the letters of solid rearranged
rum means odd or strange

explanation.surface: A solid building complex contains strange fluid tanks.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged letters wrap round RUM after their first four.
explanation.definitionFit: Oil drums are large barrels made to hold oil or other fluids, so they are containers for liquid.

clue.text: Trendy Nick providing pouch for personal keys?

blocks.note: hip means fashionable
to nick is to steal, as is to pocket

explanation.surface: Someone fashionable called Nick supplies a holder for keys.
explanation.walkthrough: Nick looks like a man's name but is the verb meaning to steal.
explanation.definitionFit: A hip pocket is the back trouser pocket, where people often keep their keys; the question mark flags the example.

clue.text: Doctor wept as nurse gets a more promising situation

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so the letters are altered in order

blocks.note: all eleven letters are used

explanation.surface: A doctor cried as a nurse landed a better job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' looks like a person in the hospital scene but is the verb meaning to tamper.
explanation.definitionFit: Pastures new is an idiom from Milton for a fresh place or job offering better prospects.

clue.text: Impression made by TV lexicographer?

blocks.note: first meaning: a hollow pressed into a surface
second meaning: Susie ..., the dictionary expert on the British quiz show Countdown

explanation.walkthrough: Susie Dent is the resident word expert on Countdown, a long-running British TV word and numbers game.
explanation.definitionFit: A dent is a mark or hollow left by pressure, and it is also the surname of a well-known British lexicographer.

clue.text: Old airline's slimmed down? It was once

indicators.note: slimmed down means made thinner, here by dropping the apostrophe

blocks.note: TWA was Trans World Airlines, a defunct American carrier, plus the possessive

explanation.surface: A former airline is said to have downsized, as it did in the past.
explanation.walkthrough: The only thing removed is the apostrophe, which slims the possessive down to a plain word.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Twas is the archaic contraction of it was, used in poems and old tales, hence 'once'.

clue.text: Box set

blocks.note: first meaning: the box is British slang for the TV
second meaning: a TV set, the receiver

explanation.walkthrough: Read together the words suggest a DVD box set of a series; taken separately each is a name for the same appliance.
explanation.definitionFit: Both 'the box' and 'set' are everyday names for a television receiver.

clue.text: Endlessly flashy man

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is cut off

blocks.note: loud means garish or showy

explanation.surface: A man who is ceaselessly showy.
explanation.definitionFit: Lou is a man's name, short for Louis, and crosswords often define names simply as man.

clue.text: Denied Lord's official a tip

blocks.note: to refuse is to deny
short for umpire, the official at Lord's, London's famous cricket ground

explanation.surface: A cricket umpire was refused a gratuity.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord's is the London home of cricket, so its official is an umpire. 'Tip' looks like a gratuity but is British for a rubbish dump.
explanation.definitionFit: In British usage a tip is a place where rubbish is dumped, the same as a refuse dump.

clue.text: "Look closely" I shout aloud

indicators.note: said out loud, the words are judged by their sound rather than spelling

blocks.note: the pronoun sounds like the organ of sight
to bawl is to shout, which sounds like a round toy

explanation.surface: Someone shouts out an instruction to examine something carefully.
explanation.definitionFit: To eyeball something is informal for staring at it hard or inspecting it closely.

clue.text: Casual woolly, back of which has faded

indicators.note: the back of a word is its final letter
something that has faded has disappeared, so that letter goes

blocks.note: woolly means covered in hair
the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A casual woollen jumper whose back has lost its colour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Woolly' looks like a noun for a jumper but is the adjective hairy, which loses its H.
explanation.definitionFit: Airy can mean light-hearted and offhand, as in an airy wave, so it is a synonym of casual.

clue.text: Discounted wine leader brought in

indicators.note: something brought in is placed inside, so it goes within the other piece

blocks.note: red is a wine
Il Duce, 'the leader', was Mussolini's title

explanation.surface: Cut-price wine is brought in by the boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leader' is Mussolini's Italian title, a crossword favourite, rather than any general leader.
explanation.definitionFit: Discounted goods have had their price cut, so they are reduced.

clue.text: Measure of substance by the sound of it

indicators.note: judging by the sound means the spelling is ignored and only pronunciation counts

blocks.note: the meat of something is its substance

explanation.surface: A judgement of how substantial something seems.
explanation.definitionFit: To mete out is to measure or allot shares, and a mete is an old word for a measure or boundary.

clue.text: Injured fore and aft at sea, one adult jumping off

indicators.note: someone jumping off leaves, so that letter is removed
at sea means confused, so the letters are in disarray

blocks.note: taken as written
A is the abbreviation for adult, and one A goes

explanation.surface: A sailor injured on a ship, from bow to stern, as someone leaps overboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fore and aft' and 'at sea' fit the nautical picture; the letters lose one of their two A's before being rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Affronted means insulted or offended, and injured can describe feelings that have been hurt in that way.

clue.text: Pro restricts French and creates a stink

indicators.note: to restrict something is to hem it in, so one piece holds the other

blocks.note: pro means in favour of
et is French for and

explanation.surface: A professional limits French imports and causes an outcry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pro' looks like a professional but is the preposition meaning for.
explanation.definitionFit: Fetor is a formal word for a strong, unpleasant smell, so it is a stink.

clue.text: German relative allowed to give punishment

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for German
an aunt is a relative
let means allowed

explanation.surface: A German relative is permitted to discipline someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Running the gauntlet was a military punishment in which the victim ran between two lines of men striking him.

clue.text: End part of sentence

blocks.note: first meaning: an aim or purpose
second meaning: in grammar, the noun receiving the verb's action

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the last part of a sentence, or the end of a prison term.
explanation.definitionFit: An object is a goal one works towards, and in grammar it is the element of a sentence affected by the verb.

clue.text: Only 20 down sauce

indicators.note: the cross-reference stands for the word 'reduced', and a reduced word has been cut short

blocks.note: just means only

explanation.surface: Simply a reduced sauce.
explanation.walkthrough: 20 down is the answer meaning discounted, and a jus is itself a reduced sauce, so the surface reads as cookery.
explanation.definitionFit: A jus is a thin gravy made from meat juices, a light sauce in French cooking.

clue.text: Ruddy strong winds ending in tragedy

indicators.note: the ending of a word is its final letter

blocks.note: blows are gales
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Fierce gales end in disaster, with a mild expletive thrown in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruddy' looks like a mild British swearword but means red-faced.
explanation.definitionFit: Blowsy describes a coarse, red-faced complexion, so it is a synonym of ruddy.

clue.text: Call James East to get good seats

blocks.note: to ring is to phone or call
Sid James was a British comic actor, star of the Carry On films
E is the abbreviation for East

explanation.surface: Phone a man called James East to obtain fine seats.
explanation.walkthrough: Sid James was a well-known British comedy actor, so James supplies his first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Ringside seats are those beside the ring at a boxing match or circus, the best places to watch.
